[0] everyday_reading (E): Folk meaning: a number is a number, so 3, 3.0 and "3" are the same value, and a variable will take whatever form the context needs (the result 'becomes' double when stored in a double). Java rule: every value has a fixed type; conversions happen only by automatic promotion to a wider type, by an explicit cast, by conversion methods (Integer.parseInt, Math.round), or by String conversion with +.
[1] misconception (M) -> NoCastIfSameSize: wrong rule: If a variable is at least as big as a value, no cast is needed to assign the value. Right rule: The compiler decides by types, not values: assigning a double to an int needs a cast even when the value (e.g. 3.0) would fit, because a conversion that might involve loss of information leads to a compile-time error.
[2] misconception (M) -> NarrowingAssignmentAllowed: wrong rule: A double value can be stored in an int variable like an int in a double. Right rule: int to double is automatic (widening); double to int needs a cast, otherwise the assignment is a compile-time error.
[3] inconsistent_trace (T) -> NoCastIfSameSize: Points to LT (each subexpression is computed in its own type, and conversion happens only where the types meet). Applied unevenly: the student promotes before an int division on one line (treating 9/5 as 1.8) but not on another, or casts the whole expression on one pass and only the first operand on the next. (here mixing in: "If a variable is at least as big as a value, no cast is needed to assign the value")
[4] misconception (M) -> TargetTyping: wrong rule: The type of a numerical expression depends on the type expected by the surrounding context, so double d = a / b; keeps the fraction. Right rule: The type of a numerical expression is determined by its operands, so double d = a / b; with int a and b still divides as ints and only then widens the result (1 / 3 gives 0.0).

[0] names_the_element (N): Type conversion is changing a value of one type into a value of another type: automatic promotion (widening), an explicit cast, an explicit conversion method (Integer.parseInt, Double.parseDouble, Math.round), or automatic conversion to String.
[1] states_the_rule (S): Java converts automatically to a type with a larger range (promotion) because no information is lost; a conversion that might lose information (double to int) requires an explicit cast or is a compile-time error; Strings and numbers convert only via methods or string conversion.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): Innermost subexpressions are evaluated in their own types first; at each binary operator the narrower operand is promoted; a cast converts the single value right after it; at an assignment the final value is converted to the variable's type (widening allowed, narrowing rejected at compile time).
[1] output_prediction (OP): Typical results: "1234" + 99 is the String "123499"; Integer.parseInt("123") is int 123; (int) 2.71828 is int 2; Math.round(2.71828) is long 3; 11 * 0.3 is double 3.3; 11 * (int) 0.3 is int 0; (int) (11 * 0.3) is int 3.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): A conversion produces a new value and never changes the source variable or its declared type: after int x = (int) pi; x is 3 and pi still holds 3.14159.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): Conversions between primitive types follow their ranges: int to double happens automatically, double to int needs a cast that drops the fraction, and boolean converts to no numeric type.
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): Parsing methods are explicit type conversion from String to a number: a method takes an argument of one type and produces a result of another.
[2] relation_to_neighbour (R): A cast is the explicit conversion between primitive types, required when information may be lost: (int) 2.71828 is 2.
[3] relation_to_neighbour (R): Widening (promotion) is the automatic kind of conversion, applied at operators and assignments when the target type has a larger range.
[4] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Adapts data between parts of a program: command-line text to numbers, int counts to double for an average ((double) sum / n), doubles to int indices or counts.

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> NoCastIfSameSize: Moving the point of conversion changes the result: (double) (a / b) differs from (double) a / b, and (int) 11 * 0.3 differs from (int) (11 * 0.3). Widening int to double and back is reversible for int values; narrowing double to int loses the fraction irreversibly.
[1] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Rely on automatic promotion when mixing int with double; write a cast only when you intend to drop information; use parse methods for text input and string conversion for output; paying attention to types avoids subtle bugs.
[2] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: A conversion that may lose information needs an explicit cast. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: Assigning or passing a double (or long) expression to an int, e.g. int n = 11 * 0.3; (possible loss of precision).
[3] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Promotion happens per operator, after an int division has already truncated. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: All-int division inside a double formula, e.g. double y = 1 / 3; or (9/5) * c + 32.
[4] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Casts work only between compatible types; a String is converted with a parse method. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: (int) str with a String str, or (int) flag with a boolean.
[5] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: A parse method accepts only a valid textual representation of the number. Kind: run-time exception. Trigger class: Integer.parseInt of text that is not an integer in digits ("five", "12.2", "").

Integer.parseInt(s) converts the String s into an int; SW later classifies such methods as explicit type conversion.
Conversion moves a value between primitive types: int to double happens automatically, while double to int needs a cast that drops the fraction.
A cast is the explicit form of type conversion between primitive types, required when the conversion may lose information (e.g. (int) 2.71828 is 2).
Widening is the automatic kind of type conversion.
